strengths: Addresses an important practical problem with a simple, useful alternative to expensive agent-based localization. The task-specific training data is a more substantial contribution than the otherwise standard retrieve-and-rerank architecture.

Reports substantial improvements on two benchmarks: function Acc@10 on SWE-Bench-Lite rises from 77.37% for Claude-powered LocAgent to 88.69%, while LocBench function Acc@15 increases from 60.71% to 76.25%.

Includes broad comparisons against embedding models, LLM rerankers, and agent systems. Comparisons using the same retriever help isolate reranker improvements, and the strong 137M retriever results are practically appealing.

Repository exclusion and source-code deduplication are sensible contamination safeguards. Filtering, data-size, and multiple-backbone experiments provide useful evidence that SWELOC training improves localization.
weaknesses: Important inference details are missing: the number of retrieved candidates, how the 10-candidate reranking window handles larger lists, ranking aggregation, and conversion from function scores to file/class predictions. These choices directly affect both reported accuracy and cost, limiting reproducibility.

SWELOC is insufficiently documented for a central dataset contribution. The exact final filtered size, collection dates, deduplication thresholds, handling of test functions and newly added functions, and a manual label-quality audit are absent. Treating every modified function as relevant and every unmodified function as irrelevant introduces noise that embedding-based filtering alone does not establish has been resolved. The promised release link is also blank.

The paper evaluates filtering thresholds and training-data choices on SWE-Bench-Lite without describing an independent validation set or model-selection protocol. This leaves potential benchmark tuning unresolved. Confidence intervals or repeated runs would also help establish the smaller gains over GPT-4.1.

The first-positive-only reranker objective is plausible, but its effect on complete rankings is not adequately analyzed. Omitting EOS does not itself establish that later identifiers remain well ranked. Comparisons with full-ranking supervision or identifier-probability ranking, alongside malformed-output and multi-positive analyses, would strengthen this contribution.

Efficiency claims exceed the measurements. Table 5 estimates token costs but provides no measured latency, throughput, indexing cost, or repository-update cost. Precomputed code embeddings do not eliminate query encoding and index maintenance. Thus the claimed latency advantage and complete deployment cost are not demonstrated.

Several results need reconciliation: CodeRankEmbed starts at 59.5% in Table 3 versus 58.76% in Table 1, and the fine-tuned 32B text reranker reaches 86.1% Acc@10 in Table 4 versus 88.69% in Table 1 without a clear explanation. Claims of superiority across granularities also overlook metrics where GPT-4.1 performs better. Combined with limited methodological novelty and evaluation restricted to Python benchmarks, these reporting and reproducibility gaps narrowly outweigh the promising empirical evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and provides concrete evidence that supervised retrieval and reranking can outperform substantially more expensive localization agents.

Results are strong across two benchmarks: SWERANK achieves 88.69% function Acc@10 on SWE-Bench-Lite versus LocAgent's 77.37%, and 76.25% function Acc@15 on LocBench versus 60.71%. Retriever-only improvements are also substantial.

SWELOC is a potentially valuable contribution, drawn from 3,387 repositories and 67,341 initial pull requests. Excluding evaluation repositories and using pre-change code snapshots are sensible safeguards.

Comparisons include relevant retrieval, reranking, and agent baselines. Filtering and data-volume ablations, together with improvements across multiple model initializations, support the value of task-specific training data.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the framework largely combines established contrastive retrieval, consistency filtering, hard-negative mining, and listwise reranking. The distinctive first-identifier training objective is not compared against pointwise scoring, alternative ranking losses, or full-permutation supervision with a defined negative ordering.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the exact final filtered dataset size, inference candidate-pool size, how windows of ten candidates produce longer rankings, and how function rankings become file and module rankings. The promised resource link is blank.

Dataset quality is insufficiently audited. Modified functions need not all be relevant to the reported issue, and test-file modifications do not establish successful resolution. Splitting multi-function fixes into separate examples can also create false negatives under the stated in-batch objective unless sampling or masking prevents this. No such handling or manual quality assessment is reported.

The evaluation does not identify an independent validation split or explain how filtering thresholds were selected without tuning on SWE-Bench-Lite. There are no uncertainty estimates, and no downstream repair experiment establishes whether better localization translates into more resolved issues. Excluding 26 SWE-Bench-Lite tasks also limits applicability to changes involving existing functions.

Cost estimates support cheaper token usage but do not establish end-to-end latency or deployment cost: indexing, repository updates, retrieval computation, and hardware utilization are unmeasured. Several accuracy-to-cost ratios in Table 5 do not reconcile with the displayed costs and Table 1 accuracies.

Some claims exceed the evidence. GPT-4.1 reranking remains better on several reported metrics, despite broad claims of superiority over closed-source models. Differences between main-table and ablation results are not fully explained, and generalization beyond Python remains untested.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem with a simple, effective alternative to expensive agentic localization. Its main contribution is task-specific training data and empirical validation rather than a new ranking architecture.

Results show substantial improvements on two benchmarks. SWERANK achieves function Acc@10 of 88.69% on SWE-Bench-Lite versus 77.37% for LocAgent with Claude-3.5, and function Acc@15 of 76.25% on LocBench versus 60.71%.

The retriever itself provides convincing evidence of SWELOC's value: the 137M model improves function Acc@10 from 58.76% to 74.45% on SWE-Bench-Lite. Improvements across several retriever and reranker initializations strengthen this finding.

Dataset construction excludes evaluation repositories and includes source-overlap deduplication. Filtering and data-size ablations provide useful evidence, and the appendix supplies substantial training details.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: contrastive retrieval, consistency filtering, hard-negative mining, and listwise reranking are established techniques. The contribution therefore depends heavily on dataset quality and experimental rigor.

Important inference details are missing, including retrieval depth, how a reranker trained with ten candidates produces rankings supporting Acc@15, and how function scores become file and class rankings. These omissions impede reproduction and interpretation.

The dataset needs stronger documentation and validation. The final retained dataset size is not explicitly tabulated, deduplication thresholds are unspecified, and there is no manual audit establishing how reliably modified functions represent relevant localization targets. Treating each modified function as a separate example also creates potential in-batch false negatives unless explicitly handled.

The cost analysis reports estimated token charges rather than measured end-to-end latency or throughput. Repository indexing, index updates, and query-encoding costs are not quantified. Precomputation supports amortized efficiency but does not establish the broader latency claims.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence. GPT-4.1 outperforms SWERANK on several SWE-Bench-Lite metrics, despite claims of superiority across granularities. Table 3's untuned CodeRankEmbed result differs from Table 1, and Table 4's tuned 32B Acc@10 differs from the main result without a clear explanation.

Evaluation is restricted to Python and excludes 26 SWE-Bench-Lite instances without modifications to existing functions. No downstream repair experiment establishes practical gains beyond localization. Confidence intervals and a separate validation protocol for selecting the filtering threshold would also strengthen the results.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution: task-specific training enables a conventional retrieve-and-rerank pipeline to compete strongly with substantially more complex localization agents.
Localization gains are substantial across two benchmarks. SWERANKLLM-LARGE achieves function Acc@10 of 88.69% versus LocAgent's 77.37% on SWE-Bench-Lite, and 71.25% versus 59.29% on LocBench.

SWELOC uses realistic issue descriptions and pre-change code from 3,387 repositories. Excluding benchmark repositories and deduplicating source code are sensible safeguards against training/evaluation overlap.

The evaluation includes numerous retriever and agent baselines, filtering and data-size ablations, negative-mining experiments, and transfer across model families. Multilingual results provide additional evidence that the training signal generalizes beyond Python.

Downstream repair and latency experiments strengthen the practical motivation: repair Pass@1 improves from 22.6% with LocAgent to 24.5%, and the same-model GPT-4o comparison reports substantially lower latency.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the architecture, contrastive objective, consistency filtering, and hard-negative mining largely follow established methods. The distinctive first-identifier reranker objective lacks controlled comparisons against pointwise, pairwise, or alternative partial-ranking objectives.

The inference procedure is insufficiently specified. Training uses ten-candidate windows, while Appendix C suggests reranking 100 retrieved candidates; window traversal, merging, decoding, and malformed-output handling are unexplained. These details materially affect both accuracy and latency.

Dataset reproducibility remains incomplete. The paper reports the initial PR count but not the final number of filtered training instances, a clear validation/model-selection protocol, or a manual label-quality audit. The code/model availability footnote contains no actual link.

The supervision introduces unexamined ambiguities. Modified functions can include incidental edits, and different relevant functions from the same issue can become false negatives under the stated in-batch contrastive objective unless explicitly masked. Filtering also favors examples already retrievable by CodeRankEmbed, without sufficiently characterizing the discarded cases.

Efficiency claims need more transparent accounting: model-serving prices, hardware utilization, indexing costs, and amortization assumptions are missing. Table 5 also contains inconsistent accuracy-to-cost ratios; for example, the 32B ratio does not match Table 1's reported accuracy. Calling inference a single ranking pass requires clarification given the candidate-window setup.

Evaluation uncertainty and scope need clearer treatment. No confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported, making smaller repair and reranker gains difficult to assess. SWE-Bench-Lite excludes 26 issues without modified existing functions, limiting claims about general localization. Improvements across complexity buckets also do not establish the claimed ability to capture cross-function dependencies.

strengths: The paper provides concrete evidence that task-specific retrieval and reranking can outperform substantially more complex agentic localization systems. Function Acc@10 improves over LocAgent with Claude-3.5 from 77.37% to 88.69% on SWE-Bench-Lite and from 59.29% to 71.25% on LocBench. These are meaningful improvements on a practically important task.

SWELOC is a useful potential contribution: it derives supervision from real issues and pre-change code snapshots, explicitly excludes benchmark repositories, and applies repository deduplication. Improvements across multiple retriever architectures and Qwen and Llama rerankers support the value of the training data beyond one model.

The evaluation is reasonably extensive, including filtering, data volume, negative mining, model capacity, retrieval ceilings, and issue-complexity analyses. Appendix F additionally demonstrates transfer to nine non-Python languages, with large-retriever Acc@10 increasing from 42.31% to 50.85%.

The paper connects localization to practical outcomes. With a fixed SWE-Fixer repair pipeline, repair Pass@1 rises from 22.6% with LocAgent localization to 24.5% with SWERANK. The latency and token-footprint experiments also provide useful evidence for the efficiency advantage.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The architecture, contrastive objective, consistency filtering, and hard-negative mining largely follow established approaches. The distinctive reranker adaptation supervises only the positive identifier, but there is no controlled comparison against alternative partial-ranking or classification objectives. The contribution is primarily the dataset and empirical demonstration.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a paper whose central contribution includes a dataset. The code/model availability footnote contains no link, and the manuscript does not clearly report exact post-filtering dataset counts, collection dates, repository manifests, or deduplication thresholds. Appendix A supplies useful training hyperparameters, but inference details for turning size-10 reranking windows into a ranking over the retrieved candidate pool remain insufficiently specified.

Experimental selection and uncertainty need better documentation. No separate validation protocol is described for choosing the filtering threshold and other settings, although their performance is analyzed on SWE-Bench-Lite. Results lack repeated runs or confidence intervals; this particularly limits conclusions about the small downstream repair improvement and close comparisons with GPT-4.1. Some cross-table results also need reconciliation, including the 32B text reranker's 86.1% Acc@10 in Table 4 versus 88.69% in Table 1.

The monetary efficiency comparison is less reproducible than the accuracy evaluation: GPU pricing, utilization, batching, and the conversion from local inference to dollar cost are unspecified. Precomputed repository embeddings are treated as negligible online cost without reporting indexing or update costs. Appendix G strengthens the latency claim, but covers only 50 instances and does not fully establish the end-to-end deployment tradeoff.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Better performance on multi-function issues does not establish that the reranker captures cross-function dependencies. Modified functions provide imperfect relevance labels, and no manual dataset-quality audit quantifies this noise. Excluding 26 SWE-Bench-Lite examples without edits to existing functions is disclosed, but narrows the supported localization scope; the limitations for newly added functions and non-function edits deserve explicit discussion.

strengths: Strong practical results: SWERANK achieves 88.69% function Acc@10 on SWE-Bench-Lite versus 77.37% for LocAgent with Claude-3.5, and 71.25% versus 59.29% on LocBench.

SWELOC is a useful task-specific data contribution. Excluding benchmark repositories and deduplicating source code are sensible safeguards, and consistent improvements across multiple retriever and reranker families support its utility.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering filtering, data scale, negative mining, model capacity, issue complexity, multilingual transfer, and downstream repair. Repair Pass@1 improves from 22.6% with LocAgent localization to 24.5% with SWERANK.
The efficient ranking formulation has practical value. Reported latency and token-use reductions provide evidence that competitive localization need not require expensive agentic exploration.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: the framework combines established contrastive retrieval, hard-negative mining, and listwise reranking. The first-identifier training objective lacks a controlled comparison with alternative objectives, leaving its specific contribution unclear.

Important reproducibility details are missing. Training uses ten-candidate lists, but the inference procedure for reranking larger candidate sets—including window traversal, aggregation, and decoding—is not specified. Exact retained dataset counts and a clear validation/model-selection protocol are also absent; the resource footnote supplies no actual link.

The efficiency comparison needs clearer accounting. Dollar costs lack an explicit pricing and serving methodology, and repository indexing costs are excluded without an amortization analysis. Describing inference as a single ranking pass is difficult to reconcile with the ten-candidate training window and approximately 78,000 input tokens per issue without further explanation.

Evaluation uncertainty is not quantified. Confidence intervals or paired tests would help assess small improvements over GPT-4.1 and the downstream repair gains. The relationship between the filtered 274-instance localization benchmark and the downstream repair evaluation should also be clarified.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence. Better performance on multi-function issues does not establish that the reranker captures cross-function dependencies. Patch-derived labels and teacher-based consistency filtering also warrant a quality audit, since modified functions need not all be causal fault locations and filtering may preferentially retain easier retrieval examples.
